Wicker refers to thin, flexible plant stems or twigs that are woven over and under each other — repeatedly, in a criss-cross pattern — to create a solid, sturdy structure. Think of how you might weave strips of paper together on a school desk: over, under, over, under. Wicker works the same way, but with real plant material instead.

The word can mean two related things, and both are commonly accepted:

  • The raw plant material itself (the flexible twigs or stalks)
  • The finished product made by weaving that material (a basket, a chair, etc.)

In everyday speech, people most often use "wicker" to describe the finished woven item or the style of weaving — as in, "that's a wicker basket" or "we have wicker furniture on our porch."

Wicker is made from natural plant materials. The most common ones are:

  • Rattan – a climbing vine-like plant from tropical forests; the most popular source of wicker today
  • Willow – flexible branches from willow trees; one of the oldest materials used
  • Cane – the outer skin of the rattan plant, often split into thin strips
  • Reed – hollow grass-like stalks from water plants
  • Rush – a type of marsh plant with long, grass-like stems
  • Bamboo – sometimes used, though it's stiffer than the others

Before being woven, these stalks or strips are usually soaked in water to make them soft and bendy. Once dried after weaving, they harden back into a firm shape and hold their structure permanently.

The finished surface of a wicker object has a distinctive criss-cross, grid-like texture — you can clearly see the lines where the material weaves over and under itself. It looks almost like a tight, interlocked mesh. The color is usually a natural tan, beige, or honey-brown, though wicker can also be painted or stained.

The basic technique is called weaving or basketry. A craftsperson starts with a framework — a set of thicker, stiff stalks called stakes or spokes — arranged in a pattern (like the spokes of a wheel, or in a grid). Then thinner, more flexible strands called weavers are woven in and out of these stakes, row by row, binding everything together.

As each row is added and tightened against the one before it, the material becomes surprisingly rigid and strong — even though each individual strand is thin and flexible on its own. This is what makes wicker so clever: its strength comes from the structure of the weave, not from the thickness of any single piece.

Wicker can be shaped into almost anything during the weaving process. The most common wicker objects you'll encounter are:

  • Baskets — the most ancient and widespread use of wicker, used for carrying, storing, and organizing things
  • Chairs and sofas — outdoor and indoor furniture, especially popular in gardens, patios, and conservatories
  • Tables — side tables, coffee tables
  • Shelving and storage units
  • Lampshades — wicker lets light filter through the gaps in the weave
  • Trays and hampers — such as picnic baskets
  • Baby cradles and prams (historically)
  • Decorative items — vases, frames, bowls
The qualities and characteristics of wicker

Understanding what makes wicker special will help you recognize it and understand why people choose it:

Lightweight: Wicker furniture is much lighter than wooden or metal furniture, making it easy to move around.

Breathable: Because the weave has natural gaps and spaces, air passes through it easily. This is why wicker chairs feel cool and comfortable to sit in, especially in warm weather.

Flexible yet strong: The weaving technique distributes weight and pressure across the entire structure, so wicker can bear a surprising amount of weight without breaking.

Natural and organic-looking: Wicker has a warm, rustic, handcrafted appearance that feels very connected to nature. It's often associated with a relaxed, cozy, or tropical aesthetic.

Vulnerable to moisture (traditional wicker): Natural wicker made from rattan or willow can weaken, warp, or rot if left out in heavy rain or damp conditions for long periods. This is why traditional wicker furniture is often kept indoors or in covered outdoor spaces. (Modern synthetic wicker, discussed below, solves this problem.)

Ages with character: Over time, natural wicker may develop a slightly weathered look — a bit like how wood develops a patina — which many people find charming rather than undesirable.

This is an important distinction you should know:

Natural wicker is made from real plant materials like rattan, willow, or cane, as described above. It's organic, biodegradable, and has a classic, traditional look and feel.

Synthetic wicker (also called resin wicker or all-weather wicker) is made from plastic or resin material that is designed to look like natural wicker. It mimics the appearance and weave pattern of real wicker but is waterproof, UV-resistant, and far more durable outdoors. Much of the patio and garden furniture you see today labeled "wicker" is actually synthetic wicker.

When people say "wicker furniture" without specifying, they could mean either. The word "wicker" covers both.
Where you're most likely to encounter wicker

• On porches and patios — wicker chairs and sofas are extremely popular outdoor furniture
  • In kitchens and living rooms — wicker baskets for bread, fruit, or storage
  • In gardens and conservatories — a classic setting for wicker furniture
  • At picnics — the traditional picnic hamper is a wicker basket
  • In home décor stores — wicker trays, frames, and decorative pieces are fashionable in interior design
  • In movies and historical settings — wicker has been used by human civilisations for thousands of years, so you'll see it in period dramas and historical contexts too
A simple mental image to lock it in

Imagine holding a long, freshly cut willow branch — thin, bendy, and green. Now imagine hundreds of those branches, stripped and dried, being woven tightly over and under each other by hand until they form the seat and back of a chair. When finished, that chair holds your weight, looks beautiful, and feels light enough to carry with one hand. That chair, and the technique and material that made it, is wicker.
